results.statement: Explain what an AI management system is and what a management system standard does

primary.title: management system
primary.reason: Definitional key: a management system is the set of interrelated elements of an organization establishing policies, objectives and processes — exactly the AIMS definition the task asks learners to state.

primary.title: AI management system
primary.reason: States the core requirement to establish, implement, maintain, continually improve and document an AIMS including its processes and interactions — the PDCA-shaped system obligation.

primary.title: Scope
primary.reason: States that the document specifies requirements for establishing/implementing/maintaining/improving an AIMS within an organization, irrespective of type or size — i.e. requirements on the management system, not on the technology.

supporting.title: Determining the scope of the AI management system
supporting.reason: Shows the AIMS has determined boundaries and applicability — useful context for distinguishing organizational scope from technical scope, but not the definition itself.

supporting.title: General
supporting.reason: Confirms applicability to any organization developing, providing or using AI products/services across sectors; supports the 'system not tool' framing.

supporting.title: Integration of AI management system with other management system standards
supporting.reason: Explains what a management system standard does relative to ISO/IEC 27001, ISO 9001 etc.; good distractor territory for harmonized-structure questions.

supporting.title: Leadership and commitment
supporting.reason: Integration of AIMS requirements into business processes illustrates management-system rather than technical control character.

supporting.title: Continual improvement
supporting.reason: Anchors the 'Act' element of PDCA referenced in the concept list.

results.note: The 'management system certification basis' concept rests on ISO/IEC 42006, which is outside the standard in scope; ISO/IEC 42001 contains no certification clause, so no primary can be assigned for that sub-concept.

results.statement: Determine the organization's roles with respect to its AI systems

primary.reason: States the requirement that the organization shall determine its roles with respect to its AI systems, and the note enumerates provider, producer, customer, partner, subject and relevant authority roles.

supporting.reason: Scope determination draws on the 4.1 context/role output and governs which requirements and controls apply - context for role-dependent applicability.
Guidance on allocating life-cycle responsibilities among organization, partners, suppliers and customers; a plausible distractor about parties' roles.
Internal AI roles and responsibilities - easily confused with the organization's external role categories, so a natural distractor source.
Assignment of internal roles, responsibilities and authorities by top management; distinct from determining the organization's role relative to AI systems.
Confirms the AIMS applies to organizations developing, providing or using AI systems, supporting the multi-role point.

results.statement: Describe the AI system life cycle and why it anchors AIMS obligations

primary.reason: The Annex A control set headed 'AI system life cycle' with the objective of defining criteria and requirements for each stage — the normative anchor for life-cycle-wide obligations from requirements through deployment and operation.
States the objective of the life cycle control set: criteria and requirements for each stage, i.e. obligations attach across the whole life cycle, not at release.

Names 'life cycle stages' as a process consideration and says the organization can specify its own stages against a generic reference model — directly the stage-definition point in the task knowledge.
Operation and monitoring control covering performance against production data, updates and repairs — the basis for drift detection, retraining and continuously learning systems.
States that risk sources arise over the entire life cycle (design, deployment, maintenance, decommissioning) — the rationale for rejecting deploy-and-forget.

supporting.reason: Mentions performance drift as a technology-readiness risk source; useful distractor context for the drift concept.
Verification and validation sits at a specific pre-release stage; a plausible mis-placement for a monitoring/drift activity.
Event logging determined by life cycle phase, at minimum during use — reinforces post-deployment obligations.
Requires a concern-reporting process 'throughout its life cycle', an example of an obligation spanning stages.
Impact assessment process applies to consequences arising throughout the life cycle; supports the anchoring argument without stating the life cycle itself.

results.note: ISO/IEC 5338 is referenced in the task knowledge but 42001's own life-cycle pointer in B.6.1.3 is to ISO/IEC 22989; an item keyed on 5338 would rest outside 42001 text.

results.statement: Explain the harmonised structure and how ISO/IEC 42001 sits alongside ISO/IEC 27001 and ISO 9001

primary.title: Integration of AI management system with other management system
primary.reason: This is the passage that names ISO/IEC 27001, ISO/IEC 27701 and ISO 9001 and states how the AIMS is integrated with other management system standards - exactly what the task examines.

supporting.reason: Annex D opening: the AIMS applies across sectors and gives an AI-specific view alongside other obligations - context for why integration is intended.
Holds the common core definitions (organization, management system, policy, risk, audit, etc.) that are identical across harmonised-structure standards; a distractor may target these shared terms.
Requires integration of AIMS requirements into business processes - often confused with integration of management system standards.
The harmonised 'management system' clause whose wording mirrors ISO/IEC 27001 and ISO 9001 clause 4.4; useful for clause-to-clause mapping items.

results.note: The harmonised structure itself (identical clause numbering of Clauses 4-10) is not stated in any single normative clause of ISO/IEC 42001; only D.2 explicitly addresses alignment with ISO/IEC 27001 and ISO 9001.

results.statement: Explain the regulatory drivers for an AIMS and why certification is not compliance

primary.reason: Scope states the standard is for establishing an AIMS in any organization whatever its role, and is voluntary in nature — the basis for what a certificate does and does not claim.
Requires identification of external issues, including the legal and regulatory environment, which is where regulatory drivers such as the EU AI Act enter the AIMS.
Requires determining interested parties and their requirements, including legal/regulatory obligations the AIMS must address — distinguishing statutory obligation from conformity to the standard.

supporting.reason: Defines conformity as fulfilment of a requirement — supports the precision that certified conformity is a narrower claim than legal compliance.
Audit definition, including third-party audit, context for what a certification audit actually evaluates (audit criteria, not law).
Notes that jurisdictions can require information to be shared with regulators — a plausible distractor about regulatory interaction within the AIMS.
Accountability objective underpins the 'responsible and accountable for its role' claim that conformity does support.
Integration with other management system standards; distractor source on how obligations from other regimes relate to the AIMS.

results.note: The EU AI Act risk tiers/timetable and the explicit statement that certification is not compliance are not in ISO/IEC 42001 text; only the voluntary-scope, context and conformity-definition clauses anchor this task.

results.statement: Distinguish an AIMS from model-level assurance and from AI ethics frameworks

Defines management system as interrelated elements for policies, objectives and processes; the vocabulary basis for AIMS being a governance system rather than a technical evaluation regime.
Requires the organization to establish its own AI risk criteria distinguishing acceptable from non-acceptable risk — the standard demands the mechanism, not the thresholds.
Shows fairness and similar ethical objectives are identified by the organization and carried into development, i.e. the AIMS governs but does not define ethics content.
Explicitly states the objectives and risk sources listed are not exhaustive or universally applicable and the organization determines relevance — no prescribed ethical metrics.
Annex D General on use of the AIMS across domains or sectors — the informative sector-application point named in the task concepts.

supporting.reason: Life cycle controls require verification and validation measures and criteria to be defined and documented, without specifying test protocols — useful contrast for model-assurance distractors.
Relationship to other management system standards (27001, 27701, 9001) — context for distinguishing complementary frameworks from competitors.
Scope-boundary determination for the AIMS; supports discipline about what falls inside the system.
Monitoring and measurement of AIMS performance and effectiveness, as distinct from model performance evaluation.

States the provenance-recording control over the life cycles of the data and the AI system, named in the knowledge statement.
States the control to define and document criteria for selecting data preparation methods, named in the knowledge statement.
Annex A control set for information to interested parties, including A.8.2 information for users — the core of the disclosure question.
States the external reporting control: capabilities for interested parties to report adverse impacts (listed concept).
States the incident communication control: documented plan for communicating incidents to users (listed concept).
States the control to determine and document obligations to report information about the AI system to interested parties.

supporting.reason: Individual acquisition/selection control already carried in the A.7 block; useful for distinguishing data controls from one another.
Guidance detailing what users must be told (that they are interacting with AI, override, human oversight) — elaborates A.8.2.
Guidance on reporting to regulators/customers — elaborates the A.8.5 obligation.
Guidance on adverse-impact reporting channels — elaborates A.8.3.
Guidance on data preparation methods, background for the A.7.6 criteria control.
Technical documentation to interested parties — a plausible distractor against A.8.2/A.8.5.
Management-system communication requirement, a common distractor against the Annex A information controls.

results.statement: Select controls for use of AI systems and for third-party and customer relationships

primary.reason: States the Annex A use-of-AI control set (A.9.2 processes, A.9.3 objectives, A.9.4 intended use) that the task requires candidates to select.
The intended-use control named in the task concepts: system used per intended uses and accompanying documentation.
States the third-party and customer relationship control set and its objective on accountability and apportioning risk.
The allocation-of-responsibilities control between organization, partners, suppliers, customers and third parties.
The customer control - responsible approach must consider customer expectations and needs.

The 'should' guidance whose illustrative objectives list (fairness, transparency, explainability, safety, privacy, accessibility, human oversight) the task insists must not be taught as a mandatory exhaustive set.

supporting.reason: Guidance elaborating the responsible-use process control; context for what a use process contains.
Individual statement of the responsible-use process control, already covered by A.9.
Individual statement of the responsible-use objectives control, already covered by A.9.
Objective text for the relationship controls; frames accountability when third parties are involved.
Development objectives control - the classic distractor when the organization is only a user and A.6 development controls are legitimately excluded.
Development process control; distractor paired against A.9.2 use process for role-based exclusion.
Internal roles and responsibilities; distractor against A.10.2 external allocation of responsibilities.

results.statement: Analyze overlap between ISO/IEC 42001 and ISO/IEC 27001 controls

primary.title: Integration of AI management system with other management system
primary.reason: This is the passage that explicitly contemplates meeting security-related AI controls through an existing ISO/IEC 27001 implementation — the basis for legitimate overlap the task tests.

primary.title: AI risk treatment
primary.reason: States the obligation to determine all necessary controls, compare against Annex A so none are omitted, and produce the Statement of Applicability — the mechanism false equivalence corrupts.

primary.title: statement of applicability documentation
primary.reason: Defines the SoA as documentation of all necessary controls with justification for inclusion/exclusion, which is what an overlap claim must survive.

primary.title: Data provenance
primary.reason: The canonical AI-specific obligation (recording provenance of training data) that an information security access control does not satisfy; supplies the non-equivalence side of the pairing.

supporting.title: General
supporting.reason: Establishes that Annex A controls are a reference set and organizations may substitute their own — often misread as licence to swap in 27001 controls wholesale.

supporting.title: General
supporting.reason: Clarifies that implementation guidance need not be justified in the SoA and may be modified, bounding how far an existing implementation can be reused.

supporting.title: Alignment with other organizational policies
supporting.reason: Requires analysis of where security/privacy/quality policies intersect AI objectives — the policy-level analogue of control overlap analysis.

supporting.title: Communication of incidents
supporting.reason: Distinguishes AI-specific incidents from information security/privacy incidents; a plausible distractor pair for 'one process covers both'.

supporting.title: Data resources
supporting.reason: Data documentation duties (provenance, categories, retention) that partly resemble but exceed information security asset inventories.

supporting.title: Operational planning and control
supporting.reason: Requires the determined controls to be implemented and their effectiveness monitored, so a borrowed 27001 control must still demonstrate AI-relevant effectiveness.

results.note: ISO/IEC 27001 itself is not in scope, so the key must rest on 42001's own integration and risk-treatment requirements rather than on any 27001 Annex A control text.

results.statement: Explain monitoring, measurement, analysis and evaluation for an AIMS

primary.reason: States verbatim the four determinations (what, methods for valid results, when performed, when analysed/evaluated), the documented-information evidence requirement, and the duty to evaluate AIMS performance and effectiveness.

The definition note the task cites: performance refers both to results achieved by using AI systems and results related to the AI management system - the basis for distinguishing AIMS effectiveness from model metrics.

supporting.reason: Definition of effectiveness (extent to which planned activities are realized and planned results achieved) underpins the effectiveness-versus-performance distinction.
Definition of measurement; context for the methods a distractor might target.
Definition of monitoring (determining status), a plausible distractor against measurement.
Documented information includes evidence of results achieved (records) - supports the 9.1 evidence requirement.
Management review takes monitoring and measurement results as input; downstream use of 9.1 outputs, not the requirement itself.
AI objectives shall be measurable and monitored, and how results will be evaluated determined - feeds what is monitored under 9.1.
Guidance on AI system and technical performance monitoring - the model/system-performance side a distractor would confuse with AIMS effectiveness.

results.statement: Explain the internal audit requirement

primary.reason: States the core internal audit requirement: audits at planned intervals covering conformity to own and standard requirements and effective implementation/maintenance.
States the audit programme requirements including frequency, methods, responsibilities, reporting, audit objectives/criteria/scope and auditor objectivity and impartiality.
Definition of audit supplies the independence/objectivity concept and the note that an internal audit may be done by the organization or an external party on its behalf.

supporting.reason: Audit results feed management review inputs — context for what happens with audit outputs.
Assignment of roles and reporting authority is a plausible distractor for who may audit whom.
Nonconformity/corrective action terms adjacent to audit findings; duplicate carrier of the audit definition.

results.statement: Explain management review inputs and results

primary.reason: Lists the mandatory management review inputs the task asks candidates to recall and spot as missing.
States what the review results must include (decisions on improvement and AIMS changes) and the documented information requirement.
Establishes top management review at planned intervals for continuing suitability, adequacy and effectiveness — the framing of the task.

supporting.reason: Monitoring and measurement results feed the review as an input.
Internal audit results are one of the review inputs.
Continual improvement of suitability, adequacy and effectiveness links to review decisions; plausible distractor.
Defines top management, the body required to conduct the review.
Policy review guidance that references management review results; a likely distractor confusing policy review with management review.
Planned handling of AIMS changes decided at review; contextual only.

results.statement: Apply nonconformity and corrective action

primary.reason: States the full nonconformity/corrective action requirement the task examines: react and correct, evaluate cause, implement action, review effectiveness, change the AIMS, appropriateness and documented information.
Defines corrective action as eliminating cause(s) and preventing recurrence — the basis for the correction vs corrective action distinction the skill requires.
Defines nonconformity as non-fulfilment of a requirement, the trigger condition the task's scenarios must be judged against.

supporting.reason: Continual improvement is a listed concept and sits alongside 10.2, but the task's key rests on the corrective action steps, not the general improvement obligation.
Requires trends in nonconformities and corrective actions as management review input — plausible distractor about where findings go.
Requires corrective actions to be considered when operational controls do not achieve intended results — related but not the 10.2 process.
Ineffective risk treatment options must be reviewed and revalidated; a distractor route for 'fix that does not prevent recurrence'.
Supplier process guidance supports the point that root cause may sit with a supplier rather than an internal process.
Control of documented information underpins retention of nonconformity and corrective action records.

results.statement: Describe the certification route and what ISO/IEC 42006 governs

primary.reason: The only element of this task located in ISO/IEC 42001 itself: the scope statement of what conformity with the document means (an organization can demonstrate a responsible, accountable approach to its AI role) — the ceiling on what a certificate can claim; certification mechanics are absent from the standard.

supporting.reason: Definition of audit with the first/second/third-party note — the anchor for distinguishing internal audit from third-party certification audit, and a likely distractor source.
Internal audit programme requirement; commonly confused with the external two-stage/surveillance cycle the task asks candidates to attribute to ISO/IEC 17021-1.
Requires the organization to determine its roles with respect to AI systems — the 'role' that the conformity claim in Clause 1 is bounded by.
Shows how 42001 relates to sibling management system standards; useful context for distractors that misattribute certification rules to ISO/IEC 27001.

results.note: Most of this task (ISO/IEC 42006 requirements for certification bodies, stage 1/stage 2, surveillance, recertification per ISO/IEC 17021-1, accreditation vs certification) is not in ISO/IEC 42001 at all; only the bounded conformity claim in Clause 1 is anchorable here, so item keys on the certification route must cite the out-of-scope documents rather than 42001.

results.statement: Analyze whether an integrated ISO/IEC 27001 and ISO/IEC 42001 audit programme can share evidence

primary.reason: The definition's Note 1 expressly allows a combined audit combining two or more disciplines, which is the basis for one integrated ISMS/AIMS audit programme.

States the audit programme requirements (frequency, methods, objectives, criteria, scope per audit, auditor selection, reporting, retained evidence) that a shared programme must still satisfy for the AIMS.
The standard's own text on integrating the AIMS with other management system standards, naming ISO/IEC 27001 — the passage that frames what may legitimately be integrated.
Requires a distinct AI system impact assessment process and documented result, so impact assessment records are AIMS-specific evidence and not interchangeable with risk assessment output.
Requires a separate AI risk assessment process; its NOTE shows the impact assessment only feeds consequence analysis, it does not replace it — the key to 'evidence that cannot be shared'.
Requirement that persons affecting AIMS performance be competent — the ground for holding that an ISMS internal auditor is not automatically competent to audit an AIMS.

supporting.reason: Inputs a management review must cover, including audit results and nonconformity trends — relevant to whether one review record can serve both systems.
Requires documented evidence of management review results, the record most plausibly shared across both systems.
Sets the audit purpose (conformity to this document and to the organization's own AIMS requirements), constraining the criteria of any combined audit.
Retention of AI risk assessment results at planned intervals — a distractor source on operational risk records.
Retention of AI system impact assessment results — distractor on whether operational impact records substitute for risk records.
Nonconformity and corrective action machinery that a single shared process could serve for both systems.
